title: Weird Animal Facts to Fall Asleep To (C1) - 3-minute sample segment
_note: Sleep-style compilation sample: our own facts only (sloth, koala, owl: scripts/animal-myths-02.json; ballooning spiders: scripts/v4-spiders.json; harvestman: scripts/myths-02-shorts/daddy.json), no new claims. Calm voice (Andrew -10%, no speed-up), very low original ambient bed (tools/music.py 'sleep', -34 LUFS), cross-dissolves only, 4-6 s holds, a chapter card per fact, one quiet ask at the start and none after. Photos: the original scripts' iNaturalist pins, CC BY/CC0 only (two CC BY-SA pins dropped).

beats.say: Get comfortable. If you like falling asleep to these, you can subscribe. Quietly. No pressure.
Sloths are not lazy. They're on the most extreme budget in the animal kingdom.
Sloths eat leaves, and leaves have almost no energy in them. Digesting one meal can take days. Sometimes weeks.
So they save energy everywhere. They move slowly. They keep an unusually low body temperature for a mammal. And they blend into the trees, so they never have to run.
They climb down about once a week, to go to the bathroom. That's the big trip. And, slow on land, they're surprisingly good swimmers.
Koalas are not bears. They're marsupials. Their closest living relatives are wombats.

chapter_card.text: The koala is not a bear

beats.say: A baby koala, called a joey, grows up in its mother's pouch, like a kangaroo.
Early settlers saw a round, fluffy, tree climbing animal, and thought, close enough. Bear. The name stuck.
They eat almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves, which are tough, low in energy, and toxic to most animals. So koalas rest, or sleep, for up to around twenty hours a day.
Owls cannot spin their heads all the way around. They turn about two hundred and seventy degrees.
Their eyes are shaped more like tubes than balls, so they can't roll them around. The whole head has to move instead.
To make that work, an owl has fourteen neck bones. You have seven. And special blood vessels keep blood flowing to the brain while it turns.
Some spiders can fly, with no wings at all.
They climb up high, lift their bodies, and let out long threads of silk. The wind, and even electricity in the air, lifts them away.
Planes have caught them nearly three miles up. Darwin found them sixty miles out at sea.
And once, in Australia, so many came down at once that whole fields turned white.
The long-legged thing most people call a daddy longlegs is usually a harvestman. And a harvestman isn't a spider at all.
It has one round body instead of two sections. It doesn't make silk. And it has no venom glands at all.
Just a tiny, walking button on stilts. Goodnight.
